hook: A strain of cockroach that copies whatever it watches sounds like a gentle oddity, and the opening sections present it that way. The real story sits in a chain of emails from one researcher to a colleague, and it pays to read them slowly, date by date. Expect dissection, gutting and human organs described plainly.
whyItMatters: The containment section sets the tone before any explanation: a buried entrance, a facility reachable only through a delivery tube, and a squad ordered to kill any instance on sight, all for an object filed as Safe. The inventory lists that follow are nothing but itemised objects, yet they let the contents do the unsettling work before the emails explain anything. Because the email writer grows openly fond of his subjects, the later messages hit much harder.
thingsToNotice:
Read the package lists before the emails, then again after: broken keyboards, a clipboard, a legal pad of scribbles and a mug reading 'I Hate Mondays' echo what Dr. Breeman taught the roaches in 2007, while the 2012 deliveries carry human organs that shift from decomposed to fresh. In the emails the insects tap the glass, mime typing, learn to walk upright, sit at doll-sized desks and fake drinking coffee, yet every test shows ordinary cockroach intelligence; they copy his motions without grasping what any of them mean.

The turn comes when one roach pins another on the table, slices it open with sharpened forelegs and scoops out its insides while it is still alive, then sits down to tap at an invisible keyboard, a copy of Breeman's own autopsy. He reports a 150% size jump and says he is putting them down, and his next message is pure keyboard gibberish with four attachments named after the coffee-mug photo. Dr. Xao's closing note admits three rescue missions failed, that the roaches grew more aggressive by mimicking the soldiers, and that some organs coming out of the tube are fresh.
